title: The Git Object Model
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose and boundaries of the git object model.
Choose and interpret a Git command relevant to the git object model using a disposable repository.
Verify the result with repository state or history and identify one safety limitation.

content.intro: This lesson introduces the git object model as part of Understanding Git Repositories. It follows the supplied Git curriculum and adds an original explanation, an inspectable command example, troubleshooting notes, and a practice task.
content.why_it_matters: Git commonly stores file contents as blobs, directory entries as trees, and snapshots plus metadata as commits. References such as branches point to objects; commands like `git cat-file` inspect them without hand-editing internal files.

content_blocks.title: Git object model
content_blocks.alt_text: A blob stores file content, a tree stores directory entries and modes, a commit points to a tree and parent commit(s), and refs name commits or other objects.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text:
**Core idea.** Git commonly stores file contents as blobs, directory entries as trees, and snapshots plus metadata as commits. References such as branches point to objects; commands like `git cat-file` inspect them without hand-editing internal files.

For **The Git Object Model**, keep the named subtopics in view: Blob objects; Tree objects; Commit objects; Annotated tag objects. Treat those as the scope of this lesson, then practise the smallest workflow that demonstrates the idea.

content_blocks.title: How to reason about it
content_blocks.text: **Before you run a command:** decide what state you are inspecting or changing, identify whether the effect is local or remote, and write down what evidence would count as success. Run after at least one commit exists. Git object IDs and output depend on repository content; do not edit object files directly.

content_blocks.title: Command example: The Git Object Model
content_blocks.code:
git cat-file -t HEAD
git ls-tree HEAD
content_blocks.expected_output: The first command reports the HEAD object type (normally commit); the second lists entries in its root tree.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Run after at least one commit exists. Git object IDs and output depend on repository content; do not edit object files directly.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Use a disposable repository. If the exercise changes state, check git status and git log before and after; discard the practice directory only after confirming it contains no valuable work.
content_blocks.limitations: The CodeLeaf web lesson page does not execute arbitrary Git commands. Run commands locally in a disposable repository with a Git version appropriate to your task. Placeholder paths, branches, commit IDs and repository URLs must be replaced with values from that practice repository.

content_blocks.title: Safety and verification checkpoint
content_blocks.text: Start with git status --short --branch. For destructive or history-rewriting operations, review the exact target, create a recovery reference when appropriate, and keep valuable work backed up. Never put credentials, access tokens or private keys in course submissions.

task: Inspect one repository object or reference using read-only plumbing commands. Record the object type and explain how it relates to the working tree, index, or commit graph.
hints: Use a read-only inspection command before any operation that changes files, refs or remote state.
After the example, verify with git status --short --branch and/or git log --oneline --graph as appropriate.
expected_output: The first command reports the HEAD object type (normally commit); the second lists entries in its root tree.

common_mistakes.problem: Running a state-changing command without confirming the target repository or branch.
common_mistakes.why: A command may affect the wrong working tree or move a reference that other work depends on.
common_mistakes.fix: Check git rev-parse --show-toplevel and git status --short --branch before proceeding.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming a command succeeded because no error was visible.
common_mistakes.why: Some Git commands are silent on success, and some expected actions are blocked by repository state or permissions.
common_mistakes.fix: Verify status, log, references, remote state or the named output explicitly.

common_mistakes.problem: Using an example placeholder literally or applying a destructive example to valuable work.
common_mistakes.why: Paths, branch names and object IDs depend on the current repository; restore/reset/clean operations can discard work.
common_mistakes.fix: Substitute real practice values, use a disposable repository, and preview changes before proceeding.

summary: The Git Object Model is covered through these syllabus topics: Blob objects; Tree objects; Commit objects; Annotated tag objects.
Choose the command for the intended effect; understand whether it changes files, the index, local references, or remote state.
Verify the result, record unexpected output, and retain a recovery path for risky operations.
